2017_104_022817mtg.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of February 28, 2017 at the Services Building. It sets the district's 2017-2018 enrollment posture against Fred Ignatovich's projection of 12,752 K-12 students — closing Bemis, Schroeder, Boulan Park and both high schools to open enrollment except for up to 25 incoming ninth graders transferring to Athens, while opening Schools of Choice for 55 kindergarten, 5 first grade and 27 middle school seats. It appoints the Board's bargaining team for TEA contract negotiations ahead of the June 30, 2017 expiration, awards $885,322.00 for ten replacement school buses, and recognizes Schroeder Elementary as one of just 329 National Blue Ribbon Schools named nationwide in 2016.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, February 28, 2017, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
Five items. The 2016-2017 Senior Scholar Athletes and the fall and winter All-State Athletes, both presented by Mike Jolly.

The Mission Moment recognizes **Katarina Tasich, a Troy Union third grader**. During December, Troy Union students wrote opinion pieces and many reached out to principal Michael Cottone; Katarina's essay argued the community should do more to stop bullying. She followed up by presenting her writing to him with concrete steps, one of which stood out — that the entire school wear black around a unified message of **"Blacking out Bullying."** The message caught on at Troy Union and then across the district, with community members wearing black in support. "Katrina is proof that we can all make a difference."

**Schroeder Elementary** is recognized as a National Blue Ribbon School, honored by U.S. Secretary of Education John B. King, Jr. in Washington the previous November. **Just 329 schools nationwide were chosen in 2016.** Principal Brian Canfield and staff receive a certificate. The fifth item adopts the Principal Appreciation Month resolution.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the January 10 workshop, the January 17 special meeting and closed session, the January 17 organizational and regular meeting, and the December 2016 Treasurer's Report.

**What the January minutes record**
The January 10 workshop heard a Section 23 proposal presentation naming two bidders — **Mondrian Properties and JP Acquisitions** — and previewed the January 17 agenda items. It ran to 9:56 p.m.

A special meeting on January 17 at 6:30 p.m., attended by Bill Bowman of Great Northern and Dana Abrahams of Clark Hill, went into closed session on the Section 23 sale (resolution 17-001, unanimous roll call) for two minutes and adjourned at 6:56.

The organizational meeting that followed elected **Dr. Philippart president, Mr. Schmidt vice president and Mrs. Fleming secretary**, all 7-0, and appointed Rick L. West treasurer. It adopted the Employment Dispute Resolution Plan (17-013), the Section 23 purchase authorization (17-015) and the $101,162.00 Global Equipment award (17-016), all 7-0, and the revised committee memberships. Mr. Hauff and Mrs. Hammond both praised the MLK Day event; Hammond thanked the Board for her warm welcome.

**Treasurer's Report — December 2016**
Total check disbursements are $10,842,523.49 — matching the register's own TOTAL REPORT line — with the General Fund group at $9,813,108.65 and the General Fund (101) itself at $9,396,917.30. Adding $1,971,606.70 of wire transfers, $157,549.67 of P-Card purchases and $32,412.94 of ACH debits, less $16,877.52 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $12,987,215.28.

**Personnel — the TEA bargaining team**
The collective bargaining agreement between the district and the TEA/MEA/NEA, representing the teaching staff, **expires on June 30, 2017**. The Board appoints **Jordan Harris as chief spokesperson** with Rick West, Mark Dziatczak, Kris Griffor, Stephanie Trotter and Dave Pass as team members, resolving further "that the Board desires to reach a fair and equitable agreement with this Association."

**Curriculum — enrollment**
Dr. Machesky presents projections prepared by Frederick R. Ignatovich, Ph.D. of STANFRED Consultants, dated February 7, 2017. Headcount has climbed from 12,056 in 2010/11 to **12,868 in 2016/17**. Projected total K-12 for 2017/18 is **12,752 excluding** self-contained special education, the early childhood program and GROW, or **12,992 including** them — then 12,751/12,991, 12,781/13,021, 12,799/13,039 and 12,765/13,005 through 2021/22. The current headcount excludes 276 students: 77 in the Early Childhood Program, 137 in self-contained special education and 62 in GROW.

The striking series is Schools of Choice enrollment, which has nearly tripled in six years: **416 (fall 2010/11), 590, 700, 821, 907, 990 and 1,120 in fall 2016/17.**

On that basis administration recommends closing **Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park** on enrollment and space constraints, and closing Athens and Troy High again except for not more than 25 incoming ninth graders from the Troy High attendance area who wish to attend Athens, with applications accepted in a two-week window at the end of March and early April.

**Curriculum — Schools of Choice**
Kris Griffor and Mark Dziatczak present. Of elementary students in 2016-2017, **552 are Schools of Choice against 5,003 non-SOC — 9.9%**, ranging from 20.8% at Hill and 16.9% at Barnard down to 1.5% at Schroeder. The SOC population is 56.5% White and 24.1% Asian against a non-SOC population that is 52.9% White and 38.4% Asian; SOC students are more likely to be Black (10.9% vs 3.6%) and on free or reduced lunch (14.9% vs 10.5%), and less likely to be in special education (3.6% vs 9.7%).

The twelve-year application history shows 860 kindergarten and 305 first grade openings advertised against 1,442 and 475 applications received, with 887 and 260 students enrolled. A sibling survey found 51 kindergarten, 4 first grade and 26 middle school siblings planning to attend.

Four resolutions follow, split between Section 105 (within Oakland County) and Section 105c (outside, where the ISD is contiguous with Oakland ISD): **55 kindergarten and 5 first grade** under each, and under each, **20 middle school seats at Baker, 6 at Larson and 1 at Smith**.

**Business**
Ten of the district's buses have reached end-of-life. Using the Michigan School Business Officials cooperative purchasing service, three proposals were obtained and reviewed with Transportation Liaison Dominick Asaro; the low bidder, **Hoekstra Transportation**, is awarded **$885,322.00** from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, under the School Bus Replacement Program funded by 2014 Bond Series 2.

Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, February 28, 2017, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Recognition — A. Senior Scholar Athletes 2016-2017 (presenter: Mike Jolly), B. All-State Athletes Fall & Winter 2016-2017 (presenter: Mike Jolly), C. TSD Mission Moment: Katarina Tasich, Troy Union Elementary Writing Assignment, D. National Blue Ribbon Award – Schroeder Elementary School, E. Principal Appreciation Month; 3. Additions & Deletions; 4. Public Communication (agenda items); 5. General – Consent Agenda — A. Minutes of the January 10, 2017 Board of Education Workshop, B. Minutes of the January 17, 2017 Special Board of Education Meeting, C. Minutes of the January 17, 2017 Closed Session Meeting, D. Minutes of the January 17, 2017 Organizational and Regular Meeting, E. Treasurer's Report – December 2016; 6. Personnel — A. Consideration: Board Bargaining Teams; 7. Curriculum — A. Report: Enrollment Projections, B. Consideration: Schools Closed to Open Enrollment, C. Report: Schools of Choice 105 & 105C, D. Consideration: Schools of Choice – Elementary, E. Consideration: Schools of Choice 105C – Elementary, F. Consideration: Schools of Choice 105 – Grades 6-8, G. Consideration: Schools of Choice 105C – Grades 6-8; 8. Business — A. Consideration: Bus Purchase; and the remaining public communication, other and adjournment items. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Recognition 2.A and 2.B.** The Board recognizes the 2016-2017 Senior Scholar Athletes and the fall and winter 2016-2017 All-State Athletes, both presented by Mike Jolly.

**Recognition 2.C: Katarina Tasich and "Blacking out Bullying."** The Mission Moment recognizes a third grader at Troy Union Elementary for her efforts to make the world a better place and to take a stand against bullying. During the month of December, Troy Union students wrote opinion pieces on a variety of topics; the students were excited about the project and wanted their voices to be heard, and many of them reached out to the principal. One topic that caught Mr. Cottone's interest was Katarina's essay — she took a risk and shared that the community should do more to stop bullying. A few days later she formally presented her writing piece to him and outlined the steps that could be taken. The ideas were good, but one really stood out: she suggested that the entire school wear black around a unified message of "Blacking out Bullying." The message caught on at Troy Union and throughout the entire school district, with many community members wearing black to support her message. The item closes: "Katrina is proof that we can all make a difference." Principal Michael Cottone and teacher Jess Bronsteen are invited to describe her efforts, and Katarina receives a certificate and congratulations from the Board.

**Recognition 2.D: Schroeder Elementary, National Blue Ribbon School.** The Board recognizes Schroeder Elementary for its designation as a National Blue Ribbon School, an award that honors Schroeder as one of the very best schools in the United States. U.S. Secretary of Education John B. King, Jr. recognized the school in a ceremony in Washington, D.C. the previous November, and just 329 schools from around the country were chosen for the honor in 2016. The item states that the award affirms the hard work of students, staff, parents and the Schroeder community, and quotes Secretary King: "National Blue Ribbon Schools are proof that we can prepare every child for college and meaningful careers. Your schools are on the cutting edge, pioneering innovative educational practices — professional learning communities, project-based learning, social and emotional learning, positive behavior systems — making you shining examples for your communities, your state and the nation." Principal Brian Canfield and Schroeder staff in attendance come up to receive congratulations and a certificate.

The recognition sits oddly beside item 7.B in the same packet, which recommends closing Schroeder to open enrollment on space constraints — the school is being honored nationally and declared full in the same evening.

**Recognition 2.E: Principal Appreciation Month.** Throughout Michigan, February has traditionally been celebrated as Principal Appreciation Month in recognition of the outstanding work of building-level educational leaders. The resolution recites that energetic and inspiring school leadership is essential if teachers, schools and districts are to ensure that all Troy students are college and career ready, and commends the district's elementary and secondary principals for their exceptional commitment to excellence.

**Consent minutes: the January 10, 2017 workshop.** President Philippart called the workshop to order at 6:00 p.m. with all seven members present — Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Miletti, Philippart and Schmidt — administrators Deputy Superintendent Dziatczak, Harris, Griffor, Gottlieb and West, and approximately 10 other members of the audience. The business services update covered the Section 23 proposal presentation and consideration, with two bidders named in the minutes — Mondrian Properties and JP Acquisitions — followed by the January 17, 2017 agenda items: appointment of treasurer, establishing fund depositories and the investment resolution for 16/17 and 17/18, portable testing tables and chairs, and bus purchases. The teaching and learning update covered special education and an update on the timeliness of IEPs, plus a professional learning update and scorecard. The workshop adjourned at 9:56 p.m., nearly four hours.

Mondrian Properties is the same firm that would go on to buy the district's Section 16 land in March 2018 and the Section 1 front parcel that September; its first appearance in these packets is here, bidding on Section 23.

**Consent minutes: the January 17, 2017 special board meeting and closed session.** President Philippart called the meeting to order at 6:30 p.m. with all seven members present. Superintendent Machesky was in attendance along with Bill Bowman from Great Northern and Dana Abrahams from Clark Hill — the consultant and the law firm named in the Section 23 item — and there were no other members in the audience. There was no public communication. Resolution 17-001 provided that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c), the Board shall go into closed session to discuss the sale of Section 23 property, on a roll call in which all seven members voted yes. The Board moved to closed session at 6:31 p.m. and reconvened at 6:33 p.m., adjourning at 6:56 p.m.

**Consent minutes: the January 17, 2017 organizational and regular meeting.** The organizational business ran 7-0 throughout. Resolution 17-002 had Dr. Philippart serve as acting chairperson to officiate until a president was elected. Resolution 17-003: Dr. Philippart was nominated and elected president of the Troy Board of Education. Mr. Schmidt was nominated and elected vice president. Resolution 17-004: Mrs. Fleming was nominated and elected secretary. Resolutions 17-005 and 17-006 appointed Rick L. West treasurer, and 17-007 adopted the fund depositories and investments resolution. Resolutions through 17-011 continued the designations of legal counsel, the superintendent as deputy secretary, the person for posting notices, and adopted the meeting schedule, each 7-0.

The recognition portion presented the Board members with the ONE Troy ensembles, the minutes echoing the script's language about members who dedicate an incredible amount of time and energy.

Resolution 17-013 established the Employment Dispute Resolution Plan applicable to all applicants for employment, all substitute employees, all nonunion employees and all nonunion administrators and supervisors, 7-0. Resolution 17-015 authorized the Section 23 sale — reproduced in the minutes in the same form it appears in the January packet, authorizing the superintendent to negotiate the terms and conditions of a final Offer To Purchase with the Purchaser on terms acceptable to him after consultation with legal counsel, and to execute it and any documents necessary and incidental to the sale — 7-0. Resolution 17-016 awarded the bid for portable testing tables and chairs to Global Equipment Co., Inc. in the amount of $101,162.00 as an expenditure of the general fund, 7-0. A further resolution adopted the Board Committee Memberships for the remainder of the 2016-2017 school year, 7-0.

In board comments, Mr. Hauff described how successful the MLK Day event was, crediting Kerry Birmingham, Dr. Machesky and the City of Troy with putting on a spectacular event; Mrs. Hammond seconded his comments and thanked everyone for the warm welcome — her first meeting as a trustee.

**Treasurer's Report, December 2016.** General Fund (101) check disbursements are $9,396,917.30, with Total General Fund of $9,813,108.65 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $10,842,523.49 — the figure the check register confirms at TOTAL REPORT 10,842,523.49. Adding ACH debits of $32,412.94, outgoing wire transfers of $1,971,606.70 and P-Card purchases of $157,549.67, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $16,877.52, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $12,987,215.28. The middle sections of the packet are the December check register run by fund.

**Personnel 6.A: appointment of Board negotiating teams for TEA contract negotiations.** The collective bargaining agreement between the Troy School District and the TEA/MEA/NEA expires on June 30, 2017; this union represents the teaching staff in the district. The resolution appoints Jordan Harris as the Board's chief spokesperson, with Rick West, Mark Dziatczak, Kris Griffor, Stephanie Trotter and Dave Pass as team members to represent the Board in the upcoming negotiations, and resolves further that the Board desires to reach a fair and equitable agreement with the Association.

The team's composition is notable: the assistant superintendent for employee services leads, with the business services head, the deputy superintendent for teaching and learning, the assistant superintendent for elementary instruction and two others alongside — the district's entire senior administration at the table.

**Curriculum 7.A: enrollment projections.** Dr. Machesky presents on enrollment projections for the 2017-2018 school year and beyond, with the analysis provided by Frederick R. Ignatovich, Ph.D. of STANFRED Consultants, the presentation dated February 7, 2017.

The enrollment history, by headcount, runs 12,165 (2008/09), 12,069 (2009/10), 12,056 (2010/11), 12,328 (2011/12), 12,391 (2012/13), 12,573 (2013/14), 12,556 (2014/15), 12,710 (2015/16) and 12,868 (2016/17) — eight straight years of growth after the 2010/11 trough, apart from a single dip in 2014/15.

The birth-to-kindergarten ratio table runs from 4.58 in 99-00 through 4.46, 4.42, 4.58, 4.67, 4.61 (04-05), 4.65 (05-06), 4.94 (06-07), 5.45 (07-08), 5.29 (08-09), 5.22 (09-10), 5.63 (10-11), 5.67 (11-12), 5.94 (12-13), 6.18 (13-14), 5.82 (14-15), 6.39 (15-16), 6.59 (16-17) and a projected 6.18 for 17-18 — a ratio that has risen by better than a third and a half over the series, meaning a steadily larger share of children born in the district's catchment area enroll in its kindergartens.

The methodology notes are explicit about what the headline figures do and do not count. The K-12 head count excludes 276 students: the Early Childhood Program (77), self-contained special education (137) and GROW, post-secondary special education (62). The projections assume 60 Schools of Choice kindergarten and 10 Schools of Choice first grade students, sibling only. Future enrollments would be expected to fall between the MOST LIKELY and LOW projections, calculated by adding MOST LIKELY plus the LOW divided by two.

The Schools of Choice enrollment series is the report's most dramatic single trend: SOC students attending the Troy School District number 416 in fall 2010/11, 590 in 2011/12, 700 in 2012/13, 821 in 2013/14, 907 in 2014/15, 990 in 2015/16 and 1,120 in fall 2016/17 — an increase of roughly seven hundred students in six years. Read against an overall enrollment that grew by about eight hundred over the same period, nearly all of the district's growth in that window is Schools of Choice students.

Projected future enrollment by grade band and year, excluding SCSE, ECP and GROW, then with them included: 2017/18, K-5 5,458, 6-8 2,987, 9-12 4,307, total K-12 12,752 or 12,992 including; 2018/19, K-5 5,370, 6-8 3,074, 9-12 4,307, total 12,751 or 12,991; 2019/20, K-5 5,320, 6-8 3,074, 9-12 4,387, total 12,781 or 13,021; 2020/21, K-5 5,369, 6-8 2,984, 9-12 4,446, total 12,799 or 13,039; and 2021/22, K-5 5,364, 6-8 2,916, 9-12 4,485, total 12,765 or 13,005. The projection is essentially flat across five years, with the elementary band shrinking slightly and the high school band growing — the shape of a district whose enrollment bulge is aging upward. The current enrollment comparison for grades K-12, including SCSE, ECP and GROW, runs 12,494, 12,573, 12,653, 12,556, 12,612, 12,710, 12,710 and 12,868.

**Curriculum 7.B: schools closed to open enrollment for 2017-2018.** Administration has reviewed enrollment for the elementary, middle and high school attendance areas. Because of the elementary and middle school buildings' total student enrollment and physical space constraints, it recommends that Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park Schools be closed to open enrollment. The district's goal for Athens and Troy High has been to maximize each building's enrollment, which has resulted in both being closed to open enrollment for the past several years; based on current projections for 2017-2018 it is recommended that both be closed again, with the exception of not more than twenty-five incoming ninth grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School, with applications for those twenty-five spots accepted during a two-week window at the end of March and early April.

The resolution closes Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park as well as Athens and Troy High to open enrollment for 2017-2018 with that exception, and provides that students with siblings attending Athens and Troy High currently enrolled in grades 9 through 11 will be allowed to open enroll to remain. The following year's list would add Barnard and Martell to the closed elementary schools.

**Curriculum 7.C: the Schools of Choice report.** Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction, and Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent, Teaching and Learning, present recommendations for the 2017-2018 school year.

The elementary enrollment projections from Fred Ignatovich give kindergarten and first grade HIGH / AVERAGE / LOW bands by year: 2014/2015 kindergarten HIGH 827, AVERAGE 807, LOW 787 and first grade HIGH 915, AVERAGE 817, LOW 899; 2015/2016 kindergarten HIGH 791, AVERAGE 763, LOW 733 and first grade HIGH 842, AVERAGE 748, LOW 802; 2016/2017 kindergarten HIGH 839, AVERAGE 811, LOW 784 and first grade HIGH 896, AVERAGE 798, LOW 876; and 2017/2018 kindergarten HIGH 863, AVERAGE 823, LOW 782 and first grade HIGH 941, AVERAGE 822, LOW 919.

The elementary SOC application history records openings advertised, applications received and students enrolled for kindergarten and first grade in each year: 2006-2007, 25 and 25 openings, 72 and 42 applications, 32 and 23 enrolled; 2007-2008, 40 and 10, 92 and 35, 49 and 11; 2008-2009, 30 and 5, 95 and 29, 46 and 7; 2009-2010, 55 and 20, 84 and 47, 62 and 17; 2010-2011, 100 and 50, 132 and 40, 106 and 30; 2011-2012, 160 and 30, 142 and 53, 110 and 36; 2012-2013, 100 and 30, 188 and 39, 117 and 32; 2013-2014, 100 and 30, 183 and 61, 98 and 27; 2014-2015, 50 and 25, 133 and 55, 74 and 35; 2015-2016, 100 and 50, 156 and 40, 98 and 15; and 2016-2017, 100 and 30, 165 and 34, 95 and 27 — totalling 860 and 305 openings advertised, 1,442 and 475 applications received, and 887 and 260 students enrolled across the eleven years.

The data summary for 2016-2017 gives, by building, SOC students against non-SOC with the SOC percentage and its change: Barnard 84 / 411, 16.9% (+0.3); Bemis 23 / 499, 4.4% (-0.3); Costello 53 / 307, 14.7% (+2.3); Hamilton 63 / 452, 12.2% (+1.3); Hill 67 / 255, 20.8% (+2.0); Leonard 45 / 394, 10.2% (+0.7); Martell 69 / 440, 13.5% (-1.2); Morse 22 / 457, 4.5% (-2.0); Schroeder 8 / 512, 1.5% (-0.2); Troy Union 24 / 443, 5.1% (-0.6); Wass 72 / 356, 16.8% (+1.0); Wattles 22 / 477, 4.4% (+0.3); TOTAL 552 SOC and 5,003 non-SOC, 9.9%, up 0.2 points. By grade: kindergarten 100 / 798, 11.1%; first 113 / 769, 12.8% (+1.8); second 83 / 758, 9.8% (-1.1); third 90 / 864, 9.4% (+0.3); fourth 86 / 920, 8.5% (-0.3); fifth 80 / 894, 8.2% (+0.6).

By subgroup, SOC students are 19.5% ELL (108) against 29.8% (1,493) among non-SOC; 14.9% free or reduced lunch (82) against 10.5% (527); and 3.6% special education (20) against 9.7% (484). By ethnicity the SOC population is 56.5% White (312), 24.1% Asian (133), 10.9% Black (60), 6.3% multi-ethnic (35), 1.3% Hispanic (7), 0.9% Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (5) and no American Indian students, against a non-SOC population that is 52.9% White (2,645), 38.4% Asian (1,922), 3.6% Black (181), 2.6% multi-ethnic (132), 2.1% Hispanic (105), 0.2% Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (12) and 0.1% American Indian (6).

Kindergarten and first grade enrollment history runs 784 and 811 (2006-2007), 804 and 793, 775 and 830, 739 and 817, 752 and 785, 727 and 832, 768 and 795, 766 and 814, 700 and 787, 755 and 728, and 798 and 769 (2016-2017). Non-Schools of Choice students by grade for 2016-2017 run 798, 769, 758, 864, 920, 894, 927, 903, 985, 875, 887, 914 and 947 for kindergarten through twelfth, totalling 11,441, an increase of 222.

A survey emailed to current Schools of Choice families asked about siblings eligible for kindergarten, first grade and grades 6 through 8 for 2017-2018: 51 kindergarten students plan to attend, 4 first grade students, and 26 middle school students — 15 in sixth grade, 7 in seventh and 4 in eighth.

The Griffor and Dziatczak memorandum to Dr. Machesky, dated February 28, 2017, lists the factors considered: current enrollment; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of SOC students currently in the district; the projected number of SOC siblings age-eligible to enter under a limited program; and available elementary classrooms. Their recommendations are to use Fred Ignatovich's 1.5 enrollment projection numbers with his recommended formula (most likely plus low, divided by two) as the foundation; to accept SOC applications for 100 kindergarten and 30 first grade students, anticipating more than 100 kindergarten applicants and allowing the district to admit 100 initially with the option of admitting more in the third week of August if space allows — noting that while this is quite close to the opening of school, some families still welcome the opportunity to enroll; to limit Schools of Choice kindergarten applicants to the full-day kindergarten program; and to accept sibling preference applications only for siblings of current SOC students, to attend Baker Middle School only, where current estimates for next year's enrollment approximate 728 and accepting 15 applications during the initial process would bring the district extremely close to an ideal total student population at Baker while leaving room to admit more in August. The memo text also notes that the actual February Count enrollment for both kindergarten and first grade was above both Ignatovich's Most Likely and Low projections.

The memo's own numbers — 100 kindergarten and 30 first grade — do not match the resolutions the Board is asked to adopt, which set 55 and 5. Portions of the memo also carry "2016-2017" where the subject line and the resolutions read 2017-2018, indicating text carried over from the prior year's document; the operative figures are those in the resolutions.

**Curriculum 7.D through 7.G: the four Schools of Choice resolutions.** Michigan law requires a resolution each school year to implement a Schools of Choice program, and Troy adopts four — the same seat counts stated once under Section 105 and again under Section 105c, distinguishing where the applicant's home district sits rather than adding seats.

7.D adopts, under Section 105 of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, acceptance of applications for a limited Schools of Choice program for 2017-2018 for 55 nonresident kindergarten and 5 nonresident first grade students who attend a school district within Oakland County, with total students including non-Oakland County residents under Section 105c. 7.E adopts the same 55 and 5 under Section 105c for students attending a district outside Oakland County where that intermediate school district is contiguous with Oakland ISD's boundaries.

7.F anticipates seats available for 2017-2018 in grades 6 through 8 at Baker, Larson and Smith Middle Schools and adopts, under Section 105, acceptance of applications for 20 nonresident 6th-8th grade students at Baker, 6 at Larson and 1 at Smith, for students attending a district within Oakland County. 7.G adopts the identical building-by-building allocation under Section 105c for students outside the county. The middle school seats are allotted per building rather than as a pooled total — the practice the district would abandon by 2018, when the resolutions read simply "14 fourteen total" across the three schools with placement based on building availability.

**Business 8.A: bus purchase.** Ten of the district's school buses have reached end-of-life. The Michigan School Business Officials School Bus Purchasing Program was used to obtain competitive pricing, which was compared and reviewed by Mr. Dominick Asaro, Transportation Liaison.

Todd Hensley's January 5, 2017 memorandum to Rick West, headed School Bus Replacement Program – 2014 Bond Series 2 – 2016-17 School Year, records that ten of the district's bus fleet have reached their end-of-life cycle; that MSBO offers a cooperative bus purchasing service to obtain competitive pricing from bidding dealers; that this service was used to obtain pricing for several different models matching the district's needs; and that after analyzing three proposals and reviewing them with Dominick Asaro, they collaboratively recommend the low bidder, Hoekstra Transportation, in the amount of $885,322.00 as detailed in the attached bid tabulation. The resolution awards the bid for school buses to Hoekstra Transportation in the amount of $885,322.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. (The memo attributes the funding to 2014 Bond Series 2 while the resolution names the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.)

Read as a whole, the February 2017 packet is the district's annual enrollment-policy meeting, and its central fact is the Schools of Choice line: 1,120 nonresident students in fall 2016/17 against 416 six years earlier. Nearly all the district's growth over that period came from outside its boundaries, which is why the same meeting closes three elementary and middle schools and both high schools to open enrollment while carefully allotting 55 kindergarten, 5 first grade and 27 middle school seats building by building. The Board also opens its teacher contract negotiation with a June 30 deadline, replaces a tenth of its bus fleet, and honors a school it is simultaneously declaring full and a third grader who talked an entire district into wearing black.
